content.title: Julio Borbon demonstrates the rarely seen 'baseball flop' [UPDATE: Brian Dozier does it better]
content.text: Ouch. In the eighth inning of Thursday's game against the Padres, Cubs outfielder Julio Borbon recoiled in pain when a pitch from Luke Gregerson struck his ankle.But here's the thing -- it didn't. See for yourself:Ladies and gentlemen, we have a baseball flop on our hands.The term comes from basketball -- an athlete might "flop" onto the floor to dramatically exaggerate contact by an opposing player, feigning injury to win a foul call from an official.But the practice of getting bendy-wendy with the rules isn't limited to any one sport. Borbon was trying to act his way onto first base, and if not for his delayed reaction, this could've been a pretty convincing performance. Unscrupulous batters have long "leaned" into pitches, and even the typically wholesome Derek Jeter notoriously pulled off a version of Borbon's stunt in 2010, successfully faking a hit to the elbow.Is this cheating? I won't pretend there's anything classy about it, but I appreciate a good flop -- if only for its entertainment value. In the NBA, where a personal foul can sway the outcome of a game, players have elevated the flop to an artform. Take a look at the perfectly synchronized "double flop" executed by Derek Fisher and Thabo Sefolosha in Game 5 of the Thunder's playoff series with the Rockets on Wednesday:(Image via SB Nation)Sheer perfection.UPDATE:It happened again. On Friday, Twins shortstop Brian Dozier turned the batter's box into a stage after an inside pitch from Cleveland's Justin Masterson. With even the announcers fooled, Dozier really committed to the bit, removing his shin guard and jogging towards first before umpire Laz Díaz could stop him.I'm pre-casting Dozier as the lead in the all-MLB production of Hamlet I've been lobbying for.-- Molly Fitzpatrick / MLB.com
